lead: A release is a controlled, versioned package of changes. It moves tested code from staging to production and carries a plan to undo it if something breaks. Releases exist because users need stable software while developers keep changing it. Mobile apps, UPI payment gateways and IRCTC booking updates ship this way. Only a few universities teach release management as a separate topic; most fold it into configuration management or DevOps. This chapter follows one release cycle.
prereq: You need: 6.6 Software configuration management and 6.4 Project scheduling; Unit 5 covers CI/CD pipelines.

blocks.text: Release scope is the list of changes approved for one release. Anything outside the list waits for the next release. Configuration management supplies the baseline; the release is a labelled snapshot of that baseline.

A version number has three parts: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR changes when the API breaks old clients. MINOR changes when a feature is added and old clients still work. PATCH changes for a backward-compatible bug fix. A build that only counts commits is not a release.

After feature freeze, no new features enter. The team builds a release candidate (RC), such as 2.5.0-rc1. Testers run the full regression suite on it. If it passes sign-off, the same build becomes the release. If it fails, the team fixes defects and builds rc2; the version number does not jump to 2.6.0 for an RC fix.

The release gate is a checklist that must pass before production. Items include all tests green, regression suite passed, security scan clean, database migration tested, release notes written, rollback rehearsed, and an on-call engineer available. QA and the product owner sign off.
Staging is a copy of production. Deploy to staging first, run smoke tests, then deploy the identical build to production. A smoke test checks login, one payment and one read path, not every feature.

Monitoring starts immediately: error rate, response time and order failures. If a threshold breaks, rollback. Rollback means redeploying the previous version, not debugging in production. Keep the last release artefact ready. Database changes must be backward compatible so old code still runs.

Release notes tell users what changed, the version and known issues. Feature flags let code ship dark: the feature is in production but switched off until a flag is enabled. A flag can be a kill switch during an incident.
The gate runs in order: freeze, candidate, sign-off, production and monitor, with a failure path back to rollback.

figure.caption: Each release bumps exactly one field and resets the fields to its right to 0: a compatible feature gives 2.5.0, a compatible fix 2.5.1, and a breaking API change 3.0.0.

examples.question: Current release is 2.4.1. The next release adds a backward-compatible feature. After that, a backward-compatible bug fix ships. Then a breaking API change ships. Give the three version numbers under semantic versioning.
steps: Backward-compatible feature: increment MINOR and reset PATCH to 0. New version 2.5.0.
Backward-compatible bug fix: increment PATCH. New version 2.5.1.
Breaking API change: increment MAJOR and reset MINOR and PATCH to 0. New version 3.0.0.
examples.answer: The three versions are 2.5.0, then 2.5.1, then 3.0.0.

major, minor, patch = 2, 4, 1
minor += 1
patch = 0
print(major)
print(minor)
print(patch)
patch += 1
print(major)
print(minor)
print(patch)
major += 1
minor = 0
patch = 0
print(major)
print(minor)
print(patch)

traps: Calling every build a release. A version number must signal compatibility, not just count commits.
Bumping MAJOR for a bug fix. A fix that keeps old clients working is a PATCH.
Skipping the release candidate and deploying straight from a developer branch.
Planning rollback after failure. Rollback must be rehearsed before production.
Confusing release notes with commit logs. Release notes address users, not developers.

quiz.a: MAJOR breaks API compatibility; MINOR adds a backward-compatible feature; PATCH fixes a bug backward-compatibly.

quiz.q: Why does a release candidate keep the same version when a defect is fixed?
quiz.a: The fix is an RC fix, not a new feature; it becomes rc2, not a new MINOR version.

quiz.q: Version is 3.7.2. A backward-compatible feature ships. Give the new version.
A team deploys to production without staging. Which two release risks increase?
quiz.a: Undetected integration defects and an unrehearsed rollback.
A switch that enables or disables a feature in production without a new deployment.

quiz.q: A payment release fails monitoring. State the first action and the artefact needed.
quiz.a: Roll back; the previous release artefact.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry release engineering now uses progressive delivery: canary releases send 1% of traffic to the new version, then 10%, then 100%. Blue-green deployment keeps two identical environments and switches traffic. Search for canary release, blue-green deployment, and trunk-based development to go further.
